extracted.intended_audience: law students, attorneys, researchers, and members of the public seeking a plain-language explanation of an administrative law doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Explain the major questions doctrine: the structural administrative-law principle that limits federal agencies from claiming broad policymaking authority on issues of great economic or political significance absent a clear statement from Congress. Summarizes doctrinal rationale and leading Supreme Court applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine (core definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The major questions doctrine is a structural principle of administrative law that restricts federal agencies from interpreting statutes and asserting broad policymaking powers of great economic or political significance without a clear congressional mandate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures that significant national policy decisions remain with Congress, consistent with the Constitution’s allocation of legislative and executive authority. (Page notes the doctrine's purpose and constitutional grounding.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear congressional mandate / clear delegation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may not exercise authority over matters of major significance unless Congress has clearly delegated that authority to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court requires a 'clear' statement from Congress before allowing an agency to make decisions of major 'magnitude and consequence.' The doctrine operates to demand explicit congressional authorization for sweeping regulatory actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigger: significance/magnitude threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine applies where the agency action concerns matters of 'great economic or political significance' or decisions of 'magnitude and consequence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an issue meets this threshold determines whether heightened clarity in statutory delegation is required. The page cites the Court's language emphasizing 'magnitude and consequence' as the touchstone for the doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation-of-powers rationale / constitutional foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine is grounded in the Constitution’s allocation of legislative and executive power (Article II vesting executive power in the President) and serves to limit how far administrative agencies may exercise regulatory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that because the Constitution vests executive power in the President and legislative power in Congress, significant national policy decisions must remain with Congress unless clearly delegated; the doctrine enforces that structural boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on broad statutory interpretation to expand regulatory scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will reject agency interpretations that read statutes to cover massive regulatory reach (e.g., millions of small sources) when Congress has not explicitly authorized such scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA (573 U.S. 302 (2014)), where the Court held the EPA could not interpret the Clean Air Act to cover millions of small pollution sources because Congress had not explicitly authorized that scope of regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on agency-imposed nationwide policy shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may not impose sweeping, nationwide policy shifts (e.g., wholesale changes in national energy generation methods) without clear statutory authorization from Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by West Virginia v. EPA (597 U.S. 697 (2022)), in which the Court held the EPA lacked authority under the Clean Air Act to require a nationwide shift in electricity generation from coal to cleaner sources, emphasizing that major decisions must rest with Congress unless clearly delegated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application in emergency/public-health contexts (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine has been applied to limit agencies' pandemic-era actions when Congress had not clearly empowered those agencies to take sweeping measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Alabama Association of Realtors v. Department of Health & Human Services (594 U.S. 758 (2021)) where the Court struck down the CDC's national eviction moratorium, and National Federation of Independent Business v. OSHA (595 U.S. 109 (2022)) where the Court stayed OSHA's vaccine-or-test mandate—finding Congress had not clearly empowered the agencies to take those actions.
